---
title: "Peer evaluation"
---

The design project is team-built, but the Engagement Credits earned during the project period will be awarded on an individual basis.

## How it works

You complete two short evaluations of your teammates — five minutes each, on Canvas:

- **Evaluation 1, end of week 12** — *formative.* The purpose is to be an early warning. 
- **Evaluation 2, end of week 14** — *summative.* This sets the project-period credits.

Both ask the same three questions:

1. For each teammate: *describe, concretely, what they built, verified, or produced.* ("Wrote and annotated the filtering module; ran the dt-halving checks" — concrete things.)
2. For each teammate: *describe one moment they moved the team forward.*
3. Anything I should know? (Free response, optional.)

A recommendation: *do something your teammates can name,* and maybe even have a discussion early about assigning tasks so that every group member does something worth writing about in the peer evaluations. This is not a "gotcha"; I hope everyone gets full credit!

## What happens with it

**The default outcome — by far the most common — is nothing.** Ordinary evaluations, including ones mentioning ordinary friction, change no one's credits.

However, when multiple evaluations can't explain what a group member is doing/did, that is a problem. I will contact the student and potentially reduce their project-period credits.

<!-- ## Why descriptions instead of ratings

Because ratings inflate — nobody wants to give a teammate a 3/5, so everyone gets 5s and the instrument reads nothing. Descriptions resist inflation for a simple reason: **you can't describe work that didn't happen.** A hollow answer to "what did they build?" isn't an accusation anyone had to make; it's just an absence, visible on its own. This also protects *you* as an evaluator — you're never asked to judge a teammate, only to state what you saw, which is a much easier thing to do honestly. -->

This is not surveillance and it's not a gotcha — it's the standard mechanism (borrowed from decades of team-based-learning practice) that makes team projects fair to the people who do the work. Team conflict that is... bigger... should not wait for an evaluation window. (Someone unreachable, someone hostile, a team genuinely stuck.) Send me an email or let's talk in office hours.
